title: Monday Launch Could Spawn “Space Jellyfish” Over Western Skies, Weather Channel Reports
body:
A spectacular aurora‑like display may light up the night skies over the American Southwest on Monday, as scientists predict a lingering “space jellyfish” will become visible after a recent SpaceX launch. The ethereal formation—caused by ionized particles spilling from the rocket’s upper‑stage engine—has already dazzled observers in California, Nevada, Utah and Arizona, and atmospheric models suggest the glowing plume could persist long enough for a second viewing opportunity later this week.

The phenomenon originates from the Falcon 9’s second‑stage engine, which ignites a few minutes after liftoff to place the payload into a higher orbit. When the engine burns, it expels a high‑temperature plume of exhaust that rapidly expands and mixes with the thin upper‑atmospheric gases. In the rarefied environment above roughly 100 kilometres, the exhaust’s charged particles interact with the Earth’s magnetic field, creating a luminous, jelly‑like structure that can drift for hours before dissipating. The most recent launch, which carried a commercial communications satellite, produced a particularly bright and expansive plume that was captured on video and quickly spread across social media platforms.

Meteorologists and space weather experts have been closely monitoring the event because the ionized trail can affect radio communications and satellite operations. While the visual impact is benign, the same ionized gases can temporarily alter the ionosphere’s density, leading to brief disruptions in high‑frequency (HF) radio propagation used by aviation and maritime services. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) issued a short‑term advisory, noting that the plume’s altitude and composition make it unlikely to pose any serious risk, but that hobbyist radio operators might notice a slight increase in signal fading during the night.

For skywatchers, the timing is favorable. The plume is expected to be most visible after sunset, roughly between 8 p.m. and 11 p.m. Pacific Time, when the sky is dark enough to reveal the faint glow against the backdrop of stars. Observers in Los Angeles, Las Vegas, Salt Lake City and the greater Arizona region are advised to find locations with minimal light pollution—such as desert outskirts or high‑altitude parks—to maximize contrast. The display will likely appear as a diffuse, violet‑blue halo expanding outward from the horizon, with subtle ripples that give it a jelly‑fish‑like appearance. Photographers are encouraged to use wide‑angle lenses and high ISO settings to capture the fleeting event.

The “space jellyfish” is not the first of its kind. Similar ionospheric glows have been recorded after launches of Russian Soyuz rockets and earlier SpaceX missions, but the recent footage has sparked renewed public interest in the intersection of spaceflight and atmospheric science. Researchers are using these accidental experiments to refine models of how rocket exhaust interacts with the upper atmosphere, a factor that becomes increasingly important as launch frequencies rise. With commercial launch rates projected to double by the end of the decade, understanding these transient phenomena will aid in mitigating any cumulative effects on the ionosphere, which plays a crucial role in global communications and navigation systems.

Looking ahead, the upcoming launch schedule includes several high‑profile missions that could generate comparable displays. If the current plume proves as enduring as predicted, it may become a regular, albeit unpredictable, feature of the night sky for communities beneath launch corridors. Continued collaboration between aerospace engineers, atmospheric scientists and public outreach programs will help translate these awe‑inspiring visuals into valuable data, ensuring that future “space jellyfish” are not only a treat for the eyes but also a window into the dynamics of our planet’s outer envelope.
